items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use well-known series to recover the sequence associated with a generating function.

Content:
One series that occurs regularly for this purpose is the geometric series

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{1-r} = 1+r+r^2+r^3+\cdots\,.]

Content:
For example, let's determine the general term [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 0] of the sequence with generating function

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{5+2x}.]

Content:
First, we rewrite the generating function by factoring out the term of the form [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1-r}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (3)/(5 + 2x)|= (3)/(5) ⋅ (1)/((1 + (2)/(5)x)); = (3)/(5) ⋅ (1)/([1 − (− (2)/(5)x)])]

Content:
Then, we expand the right-hand side using the geometric series formula:

Content:
[MATH: (3)/(5)[1 + (− (2)/(5)x) + (− (2)/(5)x)^{2} + (− (2)/(5)x)^{3} + ⋯]]

Content:
This simplifies to
[MATH: (3)/(5) + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))x + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))^{2}x^{2} + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))^{3}x^{3} + ⋯.]
Finally, we identify that the general term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence is
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{3}{5}\left(-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^n.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
In some cases, a generating function can be written as a combination of simpler functions that, in turn, can be further reduced to geometric series.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the generating function

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{2-x-6x^2}\,.]

Content:
To calculate the generating series, we first factor the denominator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{2-x-6x^2} = \dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)}]

Content:
Then, we express the function as a sum of partial fractions:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)} = \dfrac{2}{1-2x} + \dfrac{2}{2+3x}]

Content:
Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series:

Content:
For the first sequence, we have

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(1 − 2x)|= 2 ⋅ (1)/(1 − 2x); = 2 ⋅ (1 + (2x) + (2x)^{2} + (2x)^{3}); = (2) + (2)^{2}x + (2)^{3}x^{2} + (2)^{4}x^{3} + ⋯.]

Content:
The general term of the sequence associated with this generating series is [MATH: b_n=2^{n+1}.]

Content:
For the second sequence, we have

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(2 + 3x)|= (2)/(2) ⋅ (1)/([1 + ((3)/(2))]); = (1)/([1 + ((3)/(2))]); = 1 + (− (3)/(2)x) + (− (3)/(2)x)^{2} + (− (3)/(2)x)^{3} + ⋯.]

Content:
The general term of the sequence associated with this generating series is [MATH: c_n=\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^n.]

Content:
Finally, the general term of the sequence associated with our original function is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = b_n + c_n = 2^{n+1} + \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^n\,.]

sections.normalized_html: Find an expression for the general term [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 0] of the sequence with the generating function [MATH: \dfrac{3x}{(2x+1)(x-1)}.]
sections.readable_text: Find an expression for the general term [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 0] of the sequence with the generating function [MATH: \dfrac{3x}{(2x+1)(x-1)}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rewrite our fraction as a sum of partial fractions:

[MATH: (3x)/((2x + 1)(x − 1))|= (A)/((2x + 1)) + (B)/((x − 1))]

Multiplying both sides by [MATH: (2x+1)(x-1)] gives [MATH: 3x|= A(x − 1) + B(2x + 1).]

We now find the coefficients [MATH: A] and [MATH: B\mathbin{:}]

  • Substituting [MATH: x=-\dfrac{1}{2},] we get [MATH: A = 1.]

  • Substituting [MATH: x=1,] we get [MATH: B =1.]

Hence, [MATH: \dfrac{3x}{(2x+1)(x-1)} = \dfrac{1}{2x+1} + \dfrac{1}{x-1}.]

Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series.

[MATH: (1)/(2x + 1)|= (1)/(1 − (− 2x)); = 1 + (− 2x) + (− 2x)^{2} + (− 2x)^{3} + ⋯; = 1 + (− 2)x + (− 2)^{2}x^{2} + (− 2)^{3}x^{3} + ⋯; (1)/(x − 1)|= (− 1)(1)/(1 − x); = (− 1) ⋅ (1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3} + ⋯); = (− 1) + (− 1)x + (− 1)x^{2} + (− 1)x^{3} + ⋯]

The general term of the first sequence is [MATH: b_n = \left(-2\right)^n,] while the general term of the second sequence is [MATH: c_n = -1.]

Therefore, the general term of our original sequence is

[MATH: a_{n}|= b_{n} + c_{n}; = (− 2)^{n} + (− 1); = (− 2)^{n} − 1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can use well-known series to recover the sequence associated with a generating function.

Content:
One series that occurs regularly for this purpose is the geometric series

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{1-r} = 1+r+r^2+r^3+\cdots\,.]

Content:
For example, let's determine the general term [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\geq 0] of the sequence with generating function

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{5+2x}.]

Content:
First, we rewrite the generating function by factoring out the term of the form [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1-r}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: (3)/(5 + 2x)|= (3)/(5) ⋅ (1)/((1 + (2)/(5)x)); = (3)/(5) ⋅ (1)/([1 − (− (2)/(5)x)])]

Content:
Then, we expand the right-hand side using the geometric series formula:

Content:
[MATH: (3)/(5)[1 + (− (2)/(5)x) + (− (2)/(5)x)^{2} + (− (2)/(5)x)^{3} + ⋯]]

Content:
This simplifies to
[MATH: (3)/(5) + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))x + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))^{2}x^{2} + (3)/(5)(− (2)/(5))^{3}x^{3} + ⋯.]
Finally, we identify that the general term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence is
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{3}{5}\left(-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^n.]

---

Therefore, the general term [MATH: a_n] of our sequence is

Item 5 — Tutorial: Determining the General Term of a Sequence Using Partial Fractions

Content:
In some cases, a generating function can be written as a combination of simpler functions that, in turn, can be further reduced to geometric series.

Content:
For example, suppose we have the generating function

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{2-x-6x^2}\,.]

Content:
To calculate the generating series, we first factor the denominator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{2-x-6x^2} = \dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)}]

Content:
Then, we express the function as a sum of partial fractions:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2x+6}{(1-2x)(2+3x)} = \dfrac{2}{1-2x} + \dfrac{2}{2+3x}]

Content:
Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series:

Content:
For the first sequence, we have

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(1 − 2x)|= 2 ⋅ (1)/(1 − 2x); = 2 ⋅ (1 + (2x) + (2x)^{2} + (2x)^{3}); = (2) + (2)^{2}x + (2)^{3}x^{2} + (2)^{4}x^{3} + ⋯.]

Content:
The general term of the sequence associated with this generating series is [MATH: b_n=2^{n+1}.]

Content:
For the second sequence, we have

Content:
[MATH: (2)/(2 + 3x)|= (2)/(2) ⋅ (1)/([1 + ((3)/(2))]); = (1)/([1 + ((3)/(2))]); = 1 + (− (3)/(2)x) + (− (3)/(2)x)^{2} + (− (3)/(2)x)^{3} + ⋯.]

Content:
The general term of the sequence associated with this generating series is [MATH: c_n=\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^n.]

Content:
Finally, the general term of the sequence associated with our original function is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = b_n + c_n = 2^{n+1} + \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^n\,.]

[MATH: (3x)/((2x + 1)(x − 1))|= (A)/((2x + 1)) + (B)/((x − 1))]

[MATH: \dfrac{3x}{(2x+1)(x-1)} = \dfrac{1}{2x+1} + \dfrac{1}{x-1}.]

Next, we expand each of the partial fractions as a geometric series.

[MATH: (1)/(2x + 1)|= (1)/(1 − (− 2x)); = 1 + (− 2x) + (− 2x)^{2} + (− 2x)^{3} + ⋯; = 1 + (− 2)x + (− 2)^{2}x^{2} + (− 2)^{3}x^{3} + ⋯; (1)/(x − 1)|= (− 1)(1)/(1 − x); = (− 1) ⋅ (1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3} + ⋯); = (− 1) + (− 1)x + (− 1)x^{2} + (− 1)x^{3} + ⋯]

The general term of the first sequence is
[MATH: b_n = \left(-2\right)^n,]
while the general term of the second sequence is
[MATH: c_n = -1.]

Therefore, the general term of our original sequence is

[MATH: a_{n}|= b_{n} + c_{n}; = (− 2)^{n} + (− 1); = (− 2)^{n} − 1.]
